title.en: To-Karvuvu Roasts His Mother: The Origin of Cannibalism
title.zh: 托卡武武烤母：食人之始

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: To-Kabinana told his fool of a brother to look after their mother. To-Karvuvu poured water over her, killed her with hot stones, and laid her in the oven — 'I thought you said to kill her!' His brother's rebuke becomes the aition of cannibalism among their descendants.
summary.zh: 托卡比納那命弟照顧母親。愚弟托卡武武以水淋母、以熱石殺母、置於爐中烤之——『我以為你叫我去殺她！』兄斥之：『你這蠢貨，必先我而死；你的子孫從此將煮食人肉。』食人之俗，由此愚行而生。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (Dixon 1916); Tolai heritage. The tale explains (and frames) cannibalism as a curse from a blunder.

passages.text: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu were one day walking in the fields when the former said to the latter, 'Go, and look after our mother.' So To-Karvuvu went, filled a bamboo vessel with water, poured it over his mother, heated stones in the fire, killed her, and laid her in the oven to roast, after which he returned to To-Kabinana, who asked him how their parent was and if he had taken good care of her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: To-Karvuvu replied, 'I have roasted her with the hot stones,' whereupon his brother demanded, 'Who told you to do that?' 'Oh,' he answered, 'I thought you said to kill her!' But To-Kabinana declared, 'Oh, you fool, you will die before me. You never cease doing foolish things. Our descendants now will cook and eat human flesh.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The House Roofed on the Inside

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: The brothers each built a house, but To-Karvuvu roofed his on the inside; in the night's rain he sat weeding, wet and blind under the darkness, until the pitying To-Kabinana told him to abandon his house and live with him.
summary.zh: 兄弟各建一屋，托卡比納那於外鋪頂，愚弟卻把屋頂鋪在屋內。夜裡行雨，黑暗沉沉，雨水穿透內頂滴落其身，托卡武武哭訴；兄憐之，命其拆屋不必，同住自己屋中。

passages.text: To-Kabinana said to his brother, 'Come, let us each build a house,' and accordingly each constructed a dwelling, but To-Kabinana roofed his house outside, while his foolish brother covered his on the inside. Then To-Kabinana said, 'Let us make rain!' so they performed the proper ceremony, and in the night it rained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: The darkness pressed heavily on To-Karvuvu so that he sat up, and the rain came through the roof of his house and fell upon him, and he wept. In the morning he came to his brother, saying, 'The darkness pressed upon me, and the rain-water wet me, and I cried.' But when To-Kabinana asked, 'How did you build your house?' the other replied, 'I covered it with the roof covering inside. It is not like yours.' Then they both went to look at it, and To-Karvuvu said, 'I will pull it down and build like yours.' But his brother had pity on him and said, 'Do not do that. We will both of us live together in my house.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

region.zh: 新不列顛加澤爾半島（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: To-Kabinana carved a thum-fish that drove shoals ashore for the people to catch. The fool copied it wrongly, carving a shark, which ate the other fish — and would eat people too: the origin of the shark's appetite.
summary.zh: 托卡比納那刻木為松魚，投之於海使其成活，松魚驅馬利瓦蘭魚群上灘，眾人得以捕撈。愚弟欲仿之，兄明言當刻松魚，他卻刻成一鯊。鯊不驅魚上灘，反把眾魚吃光，哭訴於兄；兄嘆：『你這蠢貨，禍及子孫：此魚食盡他魚，亦將食人。』鯊魚之害，由此而生。

passages.text: One day To-Kabinana carved a thum-fish out of wood and let it float on the sea and made it alive so that it might always be a fish; and the thum-fish drove the malivaran-fish ashore in great numbers so that they could be caught. Now To-Karvuvu saw them, and asked his brother where were the fish that forced the malivaran-fish ashore, saying that he also wished to make some. Accordingly, To-Kabinana told him to make the figure of a thum-fish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: But instead the stupid fellow carved the effigy of a shark and put it in the water. The shark, however, did not drive the other fish ashore, but ate them all up, so that To-Karvuvu went crying to his brother and said, 'I wish I had not made my fish, for he eats all the others'; whereupon To-Kabinana asked, 'What kind of a fish did you make?' and he replied, 'A shark.' Then To-Kabinana said, 'You are indeed a stupid fellow. You have brought it about that our descendants shall suffer. That fish will eat all the others, and he will also eat people as well.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Qat, the Crab-Hole Stone, and Ro Lei

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖班克斯群島（象徵定位：高阿島／莫塔島）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916 (from Codrington's Mota texts)

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Qat's eleven brothers, all named Tagaro, conspired to kill him for his wife Ro Lei and his canoe. They toppled a stone over him in a crab's hole; but calling on Marawa by name, Qat was carried round about to Ro Lei and sat beside her before his murderers reached the village.
summary.zh: 卡特十一位兄弟皆名塔加羅，合謀害他以奪其妻羅萊與獨木舟。他們引卡特入蟹穴挖蟹，翻石壓之，以為他已死，便奔往村中搶妻。卡特在石下呼名求救：『馬拉瓦！帶我繞到羅萊那裡去。』兄弟抵村時，卡特已坐在妻子身邊。諸兄弟屢屢設計害他，皆不能勝。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era Mota collection via Dixon 1916; cross-ref qat-marawa-canoe (canoe episode, Codrington).

passages.text: After this, the brothers tried to destroy Qat in order that they might possess his wife and canoe. One day they took him to the hole of a land-crab under a stone, which they had already so prepared by digging under it that it was ready to topple over upon him. Qat crawled into the hole and began to dig for the crab; his brothers tipped over the stone upon him, and thinking him crushed to death, ran off to seize Ro Lei and the canoe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Qat called on Marawa by name, 'Marawa! take me round about to Ro Lei,' and by the time that his brothers reached the village, there was Qat to their astonishment sitting by the side of his wife. They tried to kill him in many other ways, but Qat was always the victor, and their plans were frustrated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916), after Codrington's Mota texts; not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and Suqe-matua Toss Up the World
title.zh: 塔加羅與蘇蓋馬圖亞拋物定善惡

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖新赫布里底群島（象徵定位：安巴埃）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Tagaro wanted everything good and would have no pain; Suqe-matua would have all things bad. When Tagaro made things, he or Suqe-matua tossed them into the air: what Tagaro caught is good for food, what he missed is worthless.
summary.zh: 塔加羅願萬物皆善，不容痛苦；蘇蓋馬圖亞偏要萬物皆惡。塔加羅造物之後，或由他、或由蘇蓋馬圖亞拋向空中——塔加羅接住的便為可食之物，他失手的便一文不值。

passages.text: In the New Hebrides, Tagaro wanted everything to be good, and would have no pain or suffering; Suqe-matua would have all things bad. When Tagaro made things, he or Suqe-matua tossed them up into the air; what Tagaro caught is good for food, what he missed is worthless. In a neighbouring island Tagaro is one of twelve brothers, and usually another of them is Suqe-matua, who continually thwarts him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and Suqe-matua Share the Work of Creation
title.zh: 塔加羅與蘇蓋馬圖亞分創天地

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: On Lepers Island Tagaro and Suqe-matua shared creation, but everything Suqe-matua did was wrong: his trees bore bitter fruit; he wanted men to walk like pigs and sleep in sago-palm trunks, while Tagaro said they should walk upright and dwell in houses. Tagaro's word always prevailed.
summary.zh: 麻瘋島上，塔加羅與蘇蓋馬圖亞同司創造，然蘇蓋馬圖亞所為皆謬：其所植樹果實苦澀；他欲人行如豬、眠於西米棕櫚樹幹，塔加羅則命人直立而行、居於屋中。二人常相爭，終以塔加羅之言為勝。

passages.text: In Lepers Island Tagaro and Suqe-matua shared the work of creation, but whatever the latter did was wrong. Thus when they made the trees, the fruit of Tagaro's were good for food, but Suqe-matua's were bitter; when they created men, Tagaro said they should walk upright on two legs, but Suqe-matua said that they should go like pigs; Suqe-matua wanted to have men sleep in the trunks of sago palms, but Tagaro said they should work and dwell in houses. So they always disagreed, but the word of Tagaro prevailed. Tagaro was said to be the father of ten sons, the cleverest of whom was Tagaro-Mblti.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro and the Hen-Dung Hair Oil
title.zh: 塔加羅與雞糞髮油之計

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Meragbuto admired Tagaro's oiled hair and asked the secret. Tagaro told him to sit under the roosting hens and anoint himself with what they threw down — and Meragbuto proudly went to a festival reeking, learning too late that he had been tricked.
summary.zh: 梅拉布托見塔加羅髮油光可鑒，羨而問其方。塔加羅答：『待雞棲樹後，坐樹下，以雞從上拋下之物塗身。』梅拉布托依言以雞糞塗遍全身，翌日盛裝赴宴，人人掩鼻而逃，方知中計，倉皇下海洗身。

passages.text: In another portion of Lepers Island, Tagaro's opponent, here known as Meragbuto, becomes more of a simple fool, and many are the tricks that Tagaro plays upon him. One day Meragbuto saw Tagaro, who had just oiled his hair with coco-nut oil, and admiring the effect greatly, asked how this result had been produced. Tagaro asked him if he had any hens, and when Meragbuto answered that he had many, Tagaro said: 'Well, when they have roosted in the trees, do you go and sit under a tree, and anoint yourself with the ointment which they will throw down to you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Meragbuto carried out the instructions exactly and rubbed not only his hair, but his whole body with the excrement of the fowls. On the following day he went proudly to a festival, but as soon as he approached every one ran away, crying out at the intolerable odour; only then did Meragbuto realize that he had been tricked, and washed himself in the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

title.en: The Endless Coconut and the Broken Tabu
title.zh: 吃不盡之椰與犯禁之死

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: Tagaro placed a tabu on all coconuts; Meragbuto devoured them anyway. Tagaro then set a half-scraped nut before him — however much he scraped, more was always left — and made him eat until he burst and died. Had he not perished, there would have been no more coconuts at all.
summary.zh: 塔加羅下令所有椰子皆禁食；梅拉布托置若罔聞，幾乎吃光。塔加羅遂取一椰，刮去一半果肉而留殼置之，誘其食盡——他刮而復刮，椰肉始終有餘，食至腹破而死。若他未死，椰子早被他食盡。

passages.text: Another time Tagaro placed a tabu upon all coco-nuts so that no one should eat them; but Meragbuto paid no attention to this prohibition, eating and eating until he had devoured nearly all of them. Thereupon Tagaro took a small coco-nut, scraped out half the meat, and leaving the rest in the shell, sat down to await the coming of Meragbuto, who appeared by and by, and seeing the coco-nut, asked Tagaro if it was his. 'Yes,' said Tagaro, 'if you are hungry, eat it, but only on condition that you eat it all.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Meragbuto sat down and scraped the remainder of the nut and ate it; but though he scraped and scraped, more was always left, and so he continued eating all day. At night Meragbuto said to Tagaro, 'My cousin, I can't eat any more, my stomach pains me.' But Tagaro answered, 'No. I put a tabu on the coco-nuts, and you disregarded it; now you must eat it all.' So Meragbuto continued to eat until finally he burst and died. If he had not perished, there would have been no more coco-nuts, for he would have devoured them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

region.zh: 新赫布里底群島麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded in R. B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 1916

source.work: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, The Mythology of All Races Vol. IX (Boston: Marshall Jones, 1916), 'Melanesia' ch. II

summary.en: To destroy Meragbuto at last, Tagaro dug a pit beneath his own house, begged his rival to burn him alive, and survived the fire in the pit. Meragbuto, 'when it is night, do you come and set fire to my house,' was burned to death while Tagaro urged him to bear it bravely.
summary.zh: 塔加羅欲除梅拉布托，先在自家屋下掘深坑覆以枝葉，再請他來縱火燒屋：『如此你我妻兒皆焚而死，你便成唯一首領。』火起，塔加羅一家鑽入坑中得生；梅拉布托醒而探視，見其無恙，竟求同一死法。塔加羅如約縱火，聽他在火中哀號，只回一句：『你不會死，我當日也是如此；勇敢忍耐，很快便完。』愚者遂被燒盡。

passages.text: At last Tagaro determined to destroy Meragbuto, and accordingly he said, 'Let us each build a house.' This they did, but Tagaro secretly dug a deep pit in the floor of his house and covered it over with leaves and earth; after which he said to Meragbuto: 'Come, set fire to my house, so that I and my wife and children may be burned and die; thus you will become the sole chief.' So Meragbuto came and set fire to Tagaro's house, and then went to his own and lay down and slept. Tagaro and his family, however, quickly crawled into the pit which he had prepared, and so they escaped death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the house had burned, they came up out of their hiding-place and sat down among the ashes. After a time Meragbuto awoke, and saying, 'Perhaps my meat is cooked,' he went to where Tagaro's house had been, thinking to find his victims roasted. Utterly amazed to see Tagaro and his family safe and sound, he asked how this had happened, and Tagaro replied that the flames had not harmed him at all. 'Good!' said Meragbuto, 'when it is night, do you come and set fire to my house and burn me also.' So Tagaro set fire to Meragbuto's house, but when the flames began to burn him, Meragbuto cried out, 'My cousin! It hurts me. I am dying.' Tagaro, however, replied, 'No, you will not die; it was just that way in my case. Bear it bravely; it will soon be over.' And so it was, for Meragbuto was burned up and entirely destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dixon, Oceanic Mythology, 'Melanesia' ch. II (1916); not verbatim.
